title: You Have $1,000 in 1929. What Happens Next?

facts.claim: Average American earned about $1,425 a year, so $1,000 is about eight months' pay
facts.note: Arithmetic on a reported average income.

facts.claim: Dow rose from 63 in August 1921 to 381 in September 1929, about sixfold
About 1.5 million Americans had an account with a broker in 1929, in a population of about 120 million (roughly 1 in 80)
facts.note: Run B, 17 Nov 2026: v2 said 'own any stock at all'. The figure is brokerage customers (Galbraith, citing the Senate count of member-firm accounts), so line 14 was reworded to 'have an account with a broker'. 1 in 80 is arithmetic. UT Austin course text gives the same 1.5 million.

facts.claim: Buyers on margin typically put about 10% down and borrowed the rest
facts.note: The doubling and $10,000 lines are arithmetic on 10% margin.

facts.claim: Many brokers required 40-50% margin by mid-1929
facts.note: Galbraith notes: 'Most brokers required cash of 45% to 50% of the value of the stocks in 1929'. Second source: ryanoconnellfinance.com/1929-stock-market-crash/.

facts.claim: In March 1929 a pool with insider participation pushed RCA ('Radio') stock up over about a week, then sold; pools were not illegal until the Securities Exchange Act of 1934
facts.note: Run B: the v2 wording 'up by almost half in ten days' could not be confirmed (one secondary source; other accounts give roughly 90 to 109). The number was removed and line 23 reworded. NYU paper: pool formed 7 Mar 1929, 'substantial insider participation'. Also https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pool_operation (12 Mar 1929, seven days) and https://sechistorical.org/museum/galleries/kennedy/lastDays_c.php (drove up the price, took gains). The on-screen chart is labelled a sketch, not to scale.

facts.claim: Dow peak close 381.17 on 3 September 1929
Prices fell about 10% in September then rose about 8% by mid-October
Irving Fisher (Yale) said in mid-October 1929 that stock prices had reached what looks like a permanently high plateau
facts.note: Source confirms the Fisher statement, NYT 16 Oct 1929; wording is the widely quoted phrase, used as paraphrase not as a quotation.

facts.claim: Black Thursday 24 Oct 1929: record 12.9 million shares
Bankers bought shares publicly to steady the market; the effort failed
Black Monday 28 Oct: Dow fell nearly 13%
facts.note: The $1,300 line is arithmetic.

facts.claim: Black Tuesday 29 Oct: about 16 million shares, Dow down nearly 12%
facts.note: Percent fall from Federal Reserve History.

facts.claim: Margin calls forced sales as prices fell
By mid-November 1929 the Dow was down almost 50%
Recovery looked imminent to contemporaries in 1930; the decline continued to 1932
facts.note: 'Every rally' is a characterisation.

facts.claim: Dow bottomed 8 July 1932 at 41.22, 89% below the peak
facts.note: $110 is arithmetic on the index, price only.

facts.claim: 1,350 banks suspended in 1930
facts.note: FDIC, The First Fifty Years.

facts.claim: Bank of United States failed 11 Dec 1930 with about $200 million in deposits, then the largest US bank failure
facts.note: historycrunch: 11 Dec 1930, about $200 million, 'then the largest bank failure in United States history', 'an ordinary commercial bank'. Federal Reserve History (banking-panics-1930-31) confirms 11 Dec 1930, New York City.

facts.claim: No federal deposit insurance before 1934; runs converted deposits to cash
facts.note: The lunch-hour scene is an invented illustration of a documented pattern.

facts.claim: About 2,300 banks suspended in 1931
About 9,000 banks suspended operations 1930-1933
facts.note: FDIC First Fifty Years table 3-1 sums to 9,096 for 1930-33. On screen each icon stands for about 225 failed banks (6, then 16, then 40 icons): arithmetic.

facts.claim: Depositors lost about $1.3 billion, 1929-1933
Average prices fell by nearly 30% from 1930 to early 1933
facts.note: $1,400 is arithmetic: 1000 / 0.7.

facts.claim: Unemployment reached about 25% by 1933
Postal Savings: 2% interest, $2,500 cap, depositors quintupled to 2.3 million by 1933
National bank holiday, March 1933
Banking Act signed 16 June 1933 created the FDIC; insurance from 1 Jan 1934 at $2,500
Deposit insurance removes the incentive to run
facts.note: Standard explanation; stated as mechanism.

facts.claim: Dow regained its 1929 high on 23 November 1954
facts.note: Federal Reserve History says November 1954; 23 November 1954 is the standard date of the first close above 381.17.

facts.claim: Insured banks display the FDIC sign
facts.note: FDIC page shows the plaque and seal; 'by the door' is typical, not universal.

facts.claim: Charts drawn on screen (Dow 1921-29, autumn 1929, 1929-32, 1929-54) are sketches of the index's shape; only the labelled figures (63, 381, 41, the dates and the percentages) are claims
facts.note: Intermediate points follow well-known year-end and turning-point levels but are not narrated or labelled.

facts.claim: The on-screen document is titled Banking Act of 1933 and dated 16 June 1933
facts.note: 'President Roosevelt signed the measure, known as the Banking Act of 1933, into law on June 16, 1933.' The president is drawn as a generic figure, not a likeness.

long.title: You Have $1,000 in 1929. What Happens Next?
long.description:
It's September 1929 and you have $1,000. We send four versions of you through four doors (stocks on margin, stocks paid in full, a bank, a mattress) and follow each one to 1933 with the real numbers.

The lead character is invented. The figures are from the sources listed below. This is history, not financial advice. Drawn by code, narrated by a synthetic voice.

Chapters
0:00 September 1929
0:24 Your quest log
0:37 The mood on Wall Street
1:00 Four doors
1:52 October 1929
2:21 Margin you
3:22 Stock you and the staircase
3:51 Bank you and the line around the block
4:46 Mattress you
5:17 The fifth door
5:32 Scoreboard, 1933
5:49 The hidden quest
6:31 Twenty-five years
6:47 The smart move

Sources
Federal Reserve History, Stock Market Crash of 1929: https://www.federalreservehistory.org/essays/stock-market-crash-of-1929
Federal Reserve History, The Great Depression: https://www.federalreservehistory.org/essays/great-depression
Federal Reserve History, Banking Panics of 1930-31: https://www.federalreservehistory.org/essays/banking-panics-1930-31
FDIC, The First Fifty Years, chapter 3: https://www-s.fdic.gov/resources/publications/first-fifty-years/book/first-fifty-chapter3.pdf
FDIC, A Brief History of Deposit Insurance: https://www.fdic.gov/resources/publications/brief-history-of-deposit-insurance/book/brief-history-deposit-insurance-3.pdf
FDIC, 90 years: https://www.fdic.gov/90years
FDIC, The 1930s (archived): https://webarchive.library.unt.edu/eot2008/20090513012935/https:/www.fdic.gov/about/learn/learning/when/1930s.html
University of Texas, HIS 315L course text: https://embed.la.utexas.edu/his-315l-external/?p=480
Bill of Rights Institute, The Crash of 1929: https://billofrightsinstitute.org/essays/the-crash-of-1929/
History.com, What Caused the Stock Market Crash of 1929: https://history.com/articles/what-caused-the-stock-market-crash-of-1929
EBSCO Research Starters, Stock Market Crash of 1929: https://ebsco.com/research-starters/history/stock-market-crash-1929
Notes on J. K. Galbraith, The Great Crash 1929: https://novelinvestor.com/notes/the-great-crash-1929-by-john-kenneth-galbraith/
NYU working paper FIN-04-022 on the stock pools of the 1920s: https://archive.nyu.edu/bitstream/2451/26529/2/FIN-04-022.pdf
History Crunch, Bank Runs and Bank Failures in the Great Depression: https://historycrunch.com/?p=14474
Cato Institute, Postal Savings: https://cato.org/blog/postal-savings-third-class-remedy
USPS, Postal Savings System: https://about.usps.com/who/profile/history/pdf/postal-savings-system.pdf

shorts.title: The Bank Run Trap of 1930 #shorts
shorts.description:
Before deposit insurance, a rumor about your bank left two bad choices: wait and risk losing everything, or join the line and help break the bank. About 9,000 US banks suspended operations between 1930 and 1933.

Full episode on the channel.

#shorts #history #1929 #greatdepression

shorts.title: Why Cash Under a Mattress Won the Great Depression #shorts
shorts.description:
Between 1930 and 1933 average prices in the US fell by nearly 30 percent, so cash that earned nothing bought more every month. The catch: by 1933 one worker in four had no job.

Full episode on the channel.

#shorts #history #1929 #greatdepression

shorts.title: The Month Every Bank in America Closed #shorts
shorts.description:
In March 1933 the new president closed every bank in the United States. That June a law created the FDIC, and from 1 January 1934 deposits were insured up to $2,500.
